title: Mammalian-scale neuromorphic learning machine near biological energy

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a neuromorphic computing system that combines human-scale numbers of adaptive processing elements, continuous local learning and whole-system computing power comparable to a biological brain while operating at biological timescales. Neuromorphic architectures bring memory and event-driven, spike-like computation together. The intended machine would learn from incoming streams during operation, without depending on a separate offline backpropagation cluster for that continuing adaptation.

Although the retained title says mammalian-scale, the proposed numerical goal is specifically human-scale: approximately 10¹¹ neuron-equivalents, with 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁵ synapse-equivalents as a proposed engineering target. Mammalian brains span a much wider range of sizes. Artificial neurons and synapses would need explicit functional definitions; counting them does not establish equivalence to biological cells, connections or cognition. A system assembled from multiple dies or packages could qualify. The defining advance is the combined capability and complete computing power budget, rather than placement on one chip.

significance.text: If demonstrated on meaningful streaming or embodied tasks, this combination would provide a substantial new capability: sustained adaptive processing at human-scale element counts within a biological computing power budget. Its significance would come from achieving scale, useful ongoing learning and low total computing power simultaneously. Efficient execution of a fixed, previously trained sparse network establishes a narrower capability.

Such a machine could also support experiments on large-scale neural computation: how distributed adaptive elements represent information, coordinate activity and learn over time. The reviewed supplementary material identifies testing neural computational concepts as an established use of neuromorphic systems. Expanding that substrate would not automatically produce a detailed biological brain model. Matching element counts and power would likewise leave human cognition and broad autonomous competence as separate scientific achievements.

Conditional downstream possibilities include adaptive controllers and autonomous devices whose computing subsystem can process changing environments within a tightly constrained energy budget. Their total power and operating endurance would still depend on sensing, actuation, communications, energy storage and other components. The biological comparison itself needs care: the supplied metabolism paper reports that the human brain uses approximately 20% of whole-body energy while accounting for about 2% of body mass. That fraction does not establish a measured 20 W electrical benchmark for a machine.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central integration challenge is to make very large numbers of adaptive elements communicate and learn continuously while preserving useful performance and a brain-comparable computing power budget. Existing evidence establishes architectural foundations and online-learning progress, but does not demonstrate this complete combination. The January 2025 review's accessible abstract discusses scaling challenges; its reviewed supplement describes algorithms and hardware implementations that support online learning. The missing capability therefore cannot be reduced to an absence of local-learning methods.

Engineering synthesis: the hardware must accommodate the proposed adaptive state and connectivity while keeping memory access, spike routing, synchronization and learning updates within the total power budget. Scaling element counts alone would be insufficient if communication congestion, insufficient connectivity or slow updates prevented useful operation at the declared biological rates. Multiple dies and packages remain acceptable, but their interconnects and supporting equipment must fit the same performance and power requirements.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: local update rules must produce useful adaptation across changing streams, retain earlier capabilities and avoid unstable activity or destructive interference. A scalable software and measurement stack must expose those learning behaviors and account for all supporting computation. These are concrete requirements of the proposed machine, rather than findings established in detail by the retained Nature main article: the supplied review had access only to its subscription preview and complete supplement.

current_state.text: In its April 17, 2024 announcement, Intel described Hala Point as the world's largest neuromorphic system. Intel reported capacity for up to 1.15 billion neurons and 128 billion synapses across 140,544 neuromorphic processing cores, with maximum system power of 2,600 W. It compared the neuron capacity with an owl brain or the cortex of a capuchin monkey. These are dated vendor-reported specifications and capacity analogies, rather than independent verification of human-scale continuous learning at biological power. The maximum-power figure does not specify consumption during a particular learning workload or at a particular biological spike rate.

The 2009 human-brain review reports an estimate of approximately 86 billion neurons and 85 billion non-neuronal cells in adult male brains. Relative to that neuron estimate, Hala Point's reported capacity is about 75 times smaller. Intel also reported that its full neuron capacity could execute up to 20 times faster than a human brain and stated that Hala Point was not intended for neuroscience modeling. These comparisons do not make its simplified neuron models functionally equivalent to biological neurons; dividing its watts by neuron capacity and comparing the result directly with human metabolism would obscure differences in models, workloads and operating rates.

Intel's reported efficiency of 15 TOPS/W concerned a sparse 8-bit deep-network workload. The characterized multilayer perceptron used 10:1 pruning sparsity and sigma-delta neuron models with 10% activation rates. This is relevant evidence of selected-workload efficiency, but it does not establish continuous local learning at the proposed scale and whole-system biological power. The announcement presented large-scale real-time continuous learning as a future possibility.

The January 22, 2025 Nature review, Neuromorphic computing at scale, supplies additional evidence of progress through its reviewed supplementary document. That supplement describes DECOLLE, e-prop and hardware implementations supporting online learning, together with progress toward continual learning. It also reports that SpiNNaker-2, released in 2022, was undergoing expansion toward 720 boards and a target of 5.2 billion neurons. The expansion is a reported target, not evidence that the larger system was completed. The retained main article is a subscription preview; the complete supplementary document does not substitute for access to the main technical discussion.

The supplied evidence does not establish the largest neuromorphic system as of November 1, 2026, or whether any later system has achieved the complete proposed combination. The supplied review contains no freshness search record capable of settling those questions. This limits present-day conclusions; it does not invalidate the dated Hala Point specifications or establish that later advances did not occur.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scale criterion: demonstrate an operational system with on the order of 10¹¹ neuron-equivalents, anchored to the reported human estimate of approximately 86 billion neurons, and 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁵ synapse-equivalents. The synapse range is a proposed engineering target; the supplied sources do not establish its proximity to the human whole-brain synapse count. Before testing, define each equivalent's state, dynamics, precision, connectivity and learning capability, and distinguish provisioned capacity from elements actively participating in the demonstration. These are proposed criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed scale criterion

completion_criteria.text: Proposed power criterion: measure complete computing-system power while the system performs the declared learning workload at specified biological spike rates and response times. Set an explicit watt threshold with a stated biological and measurement basis before testing; the supplied metabolic energy fraction alone cannot determine it. The proposed measurement boundary should account for memory, interconnects, host support, power conversion and cooling needed to sustain operation. Report the power of sensors and actuators separately if the demonstration uses a robot.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed power criterion

completion_criteria.text: Proposed learning criterion: demonstrate useful continuous local adaptation on streaming or embodied tasks without relying on a separate offline backpropagation cluster for that adaptation. Specify operating duration, incoming data rate, task changes, learning quality, retention of earlier capabilities and recovery from interference. Disclose any pretraining, external computation or periodic retraining so that the demonstrated contribution of local learning is clear. A sparse-network throughput or TOPS/W result alone would not satisfy this combined criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed learning criterion

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criterion: publish sufficient hardware definitions, learning rules, workloads, configurations and power-measurement procedures for independent teams to reproduce the core results. Repeat measurements across declared activity levels and task changes, and report failures and practical limits alongside successes. Multiple dies or packages may qualify if their complete computing system meets the criteria. Finite experiments would establish demonstrated breadth over those conditions, rather than universal learning ability, human cognition or biological fidelity.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility criterion

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CPE-03, General-purpose fabric that retires data-movement dominance, has the closest architectural overlap because neuromorphic systems integrate memory and computation. CPE-05 specifically requires continuous adaptive learning at human-scale element counts and biological computing power. Success on those requirements would not by itself establish a general-purpose solution to data-movement dominance, while a successful CPE-03 fabric need not implement spiking computation or local learning.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-02, Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer, and CPE-06, Wall-plug-superior superconducting classical computer at useful scale, share an interest in computing energy. Their defining advances concern different physical computing approaches and efficiency conditions. CPE-05 does not require reversible or superconducting operation, and either approach would still need to demonstrate the specified learning, scale and total computing power to satisfy CPE-05.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-04, Cascadable general-purpose photonic computer with optical memory, could overlap through possible communication, memory or processing substrates. CPE-08, Economically manufacturable atomic-density defect-tolerant digital computer, could overlap through dense adaptive-state storage or computation. Neither roster entry's defining physical or manufacturing capability entails continuous local learning near biological energy. Conversely, CPE-05 does not require optical memory or atomic-density digital construction.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-01, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer, concerns reliable quantum computation; CPE-07, Utility-scale quantum-repeater internet, concerns quantum networking. Neither capability is a requirement of the proposed neuromorphic learning machine, and achieving CPE-05 would not establish either quantum capability. All remain distinct entries.

CPE-05 also overlaps continual-learning algorithms, robotics and computational neuroscience. Algorithms supply adaptation mechanisms, robotics supplies demanding streams of sensing and action, and neuroscience supplies computational questions and biological reference points. The defining contribution here is their integration through computing hardware, memory, communication and learning systems. The research's reference to historical item 4 cannot be matched confidently to another concept because that historical item was not supplied.

change_log.change: Preserved CPE-05 and its title while clarifying that the proposed numerical target is specifically human-scale.
change_log.reason: Mammalian brains span many sizes; the approximately 10¹¹-neuron target is anchored to the supplied human estimate.

change_log.change: Replaced an undated largest-system assertion and general kilowatt characterization with Intel's April 2024 Hala Point specifications.
change_log.reason: A dated vendor announcement supports one system's capacity and maximum power, not a 2026 ranking or a power claim about all neuromorphic systems.

change_log.change: Integrated Hala Point's neuron, synapse, core, speed and workload details with limits on biological comparisons.
change_log.reason: These details explain the demonstrated scale and efficiency without treating artificial neuron capacity as biological or cognitive equivalence.

change_log.change: Distinguished demonstrated online-learning progress from the proposed integrated continuous-learning capability.
change_log.reason: The reviewed Nature supplement describes online-learning algorithms and implementations; claiming that local learning is absent would discard relevant progress.

change_log.change: Preserved the Nature access limitation and separated the SpiNNaker-2 expansion target from a completed demonstration.
change_log.reason: The main article was available only as a preview, and a planned 5.2-billion-neuron system does not establish its completion.

change_log.change: Recast the synapse range as a proposed engineering target and removed an implied verified 20 W benchmark.
change_log.reason: The supplied sources establish neither the claimed human synapse-count proximity nor a measured electrical watt threshold.

change_log.change: Separated direct adaptive-computing consequences from conditional robotics, cognition and neuroscience outcomes.
change_log.reason: Computing power does not determine total robot endurance, and element counts do not establish human cognition or detailed biological fidelity.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion demonstrations to cover equivalence, active capacity, learning quality, retention, operating conditions, power boundaries and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: The integrated goal needs testable conditions without presenting proposed thresholds as consensus standards or finite tests as universal proof.

change_log.change: Explained distinctions with every other supplied roster entry and retained uncertainty about historical item 4.
change_log.reason: The roster supports conceptual comparisons, but the absent historical item cannot support a verified identity or packaging requirement.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system achieved the complete proposed combination by November 1, 2026, and which system then had the largest relevant capacity, remain unresolved because the supplied freshness search record is empty.

The retained Nature main article is a subscription preview. Its detailed software and local-learning analysis, including the candidate's proposed quotation, could not be verified from that preview; the complete supplement supports narrower conclusions.
Artificial neuron and synapse equivalence, required connectivity and the relationship between provisioned capacity and actively useful adaptive elements still require operational definitions.
The proposed 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁵ synapse-equivalent range lacks a supplied biological whole-brain synapse-count anchor.
A numerical biological-power threshold and its measurement boundary remain to be justified; approximately 20% of whole-body energy use does not alone specify electrical watts.
Learning-quality, retention, duration and task-breadth thresholds remain proposals requiring explicit selection before a convincing demonstration.
The supplied record does not independently verify every vendor performance claim or establish Hala Point's power during a specified continuous-learning workload.
Historical item 4 was not supplied, so its identity and alleged single-chip or single-package requirement cannot be verified.
